BERT generates soft labels to guide seq2seq ASR training. It also utilizes context beyond the current utterance as input. Experiments on Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ) demonstrate significant ASR performance improvement over the seq2seq baseline. BERT distillation outperforms transformer LM left-context-only distillation. Multi-utterance context utility is also confirmed. This method surpasses other LM integration approaches (n-best rescoring, shallow fusion) without incurring extra inference cost.

author: Gray
title: Projector Ensemble for Enhanced Feature Distillation
abstract: Existing approaches in knowledge distillation, particularly for feature distillation, typically emphasize the formulation of loss functions and the choice of layers for knowledge transfer. However, the role played by the feature projector connecting the student and teacher networks has received insufficient investigation. This work initially examines a credible operational mechanism of the projector, supported by empirical observations. Subsequently, a novel feature distillation technique is introduced, leveraging an ensemble of projectors to achieve additional performance gains. Our findings indicate a beneficial impact of employing a projector for the student network, even when the feature dimensions of the student and teacher are identical. When a projector is absent, training the student backbone can be conceptualized as a multi-task learning scenario. This involves simultaneously accomplishing discriminative feature extraction for classification and the task of feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation. We postulate, and subsequently validate through experimentation, that in the absence of a projector, the student network exhibits a tendency to overfit the feature distributions provided by the teacher, notwithstanding differences in their architectural design and initial weight configurations. Consequently, the student's advanced features, subsequently leveraged for classification, suffer a reduction in quality. Conversely, the inclusion of a projector serves to decouple these two learning tasks. This allows the student network to concentrate more effectively on its primary objective of feature extraction, while simultaneously leveraging the teacher's features as a form of guidance via the projector. Inspired by the observed beneficial impact of the projector within feature distillation, we introduce the concept of combining multiple projectors into an ensemble, aiming to further enhance the quality of features learned by the student. Empirical evaluations conducted across various datasets and numerous teacher-student network pairings demonstrate the efficacy of the presented approach.

author: Mayo
title: An Investigation into Bias-Variance Dynamics of Soft Labels in Knowledge Distillation
abstract:
Soft labels, derived from a teacher network's outputs, play a crucial role in supervising student network training during knowledge distillation, an effective strategy leveraging well-trained models or ensembles. While prior work has established the regularization benefits of soft labels for student models, implying a reduction in variance within a statistical learning framework, the precise modifications to both bias and variance during this soft-label-guided training remain underexplored. Our investigation delves into the specific bias-variance tradeoffs associated with soft-label distillation. We pinpoint two crucial observations: first, the bias-variance equilibrium shifts differently for individual samples throughout the training process. Second, holding the distillation temperature constant, we noted an inverse relationship between distillation efficacy and the quantity of certain samples. These 'regularization samples' are characterized by simultaneously elevating bias and diminishing variance. However, our empirical data indicates that simply removing these regularization samples entirely degrades distillation performance. These findings prompt the development of novel weighted soft labels, designed to assist the network in managing the individual sample-level bias-variance tradeoff adaptively. The efficacy of our approach is confirmed through experiments conducted on established evaluation benchmarks. Source code for our implementation is accessible at 

https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation

author: Bowman
title: Generating Compact Universal Paralinguistic Speech Embeddings via Distillation
abstract: While self-supervised techniques have recently enhanced speech representation quality, their widespread deployment faces hurdles due to the significant computational resources required by state-of-the-art embedding models and their limited public availability. This investigation addresses these challenges by introducing and making publicly accessible a set of paralinguistic speech models. These models are characterized by their compact size and performance levels approaching state-of-the-art. Our methodology is founded on knowledge distillation, and the training of these models relies exclusively on public datasets. Various architectural designs are explored, and a comprehensive evaluation of our models is conducted against the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. The largest model derived through distillation occupies less than 15% of the original model's storage (314MB versus 2.2GB). It achieves greater than 96% of the accuracy across 6 out of 7 tasks and was trained using merely 6.5% of the initial dataset volume. Our most compact model is 1% the size, at 22MB, and yields over 90% of the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. These models demonstrate superior performance compared to the open-source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks. Furthermore, our smallest model surpasses the open-source Wav2Vec 2.0 in both emotion recognition tasks, despite being only 7% its size.

author: Hawkins
title: An Efficient Knowledge Distillation Approach for Visual Recognition Tasks
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) proves beneficial across various visual recognition challenges, including supervised classification and the development of self-supervised representations. However, standard KD configurations often impose substantial computational burdens. This is largely because their process entails extensive forwarding through large teacher networks, leading to an overall learning pipeline that is both slow and expensive. A prior solution, ReLabel, proposed to address this by generating a full image label map. During its training, it derives region-level labels for cropped regions through RoI alignment on a previously formed global label map, thereby efficiently creating supervision without repeated passes through the teachers. However, given that ReLabel's KD teachers stem from conventional multi-crop training, discrepancies emerge between the overall label map and the specific region-level labels, leading to a decline in performance. We present an efficient knowledge distillation approach that accurately simulates the distillation training stage. This method produces soft labels via the multi-crop KD methodology. Its training speed surpasses ReLabel's, as it avoids post-processing operations like RoI align and softmax. Our framework even exceeds the efficiency of traditional image classification when multiple crops are loaded from a single image. On ImageNet-1K, our method with ResNet-50 achieves 79.8% accuracy, exceeding ReLabel by roughly 1.0% and being faster. We also establish its efficiency advantage in self-supervised learning.

author: Cohen
title: An Attention-Driven Approach for Intermediate Layer Projection in Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation entails pairing a larger teacher neural network with a more compact student network during training, serving as a dual strategy for model compression and performance preservation. In this setup, the student network endeavors to replicate the outputs of the teacher, which functions as a dependable source of predictions. A common limitation is that this supervisory signal is typically restricted to the model's ultimate predictions. However, internal components of the student architecture could also gain valuable guidance from the teacher's intermediate representations. Our investigation addresses the challenge of distilling knowledge from intermediate layers. A significant hurdle in this domain arises from the lack of direct correspondence between the layers of the student and teacher networks. Current methodologies often bypass certain teacher layers, extracting knowledge from only a select few, a practice that noticeably diminishes performance. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel combinatorial approach that incorporates attention mechanisms. This method actively combines information from the teacher's various layers, assigning weight based on their individual importance, before projecting this aggregated knowledge onto the student's layers for distillation. For empirical validation, we applied this method to distill a 12-layer BERT model (Devlin et al. 2019) into student models comprising 6, 4, and 2 layers. Performance was benchmarked across standard GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Our findings indicate that this attention-based combinatorial strategy consistently surpasses the efficacy of alternative established distillation techniques.

author: Cameron
title: Enhanced Learning for Compact Models through Pre-training: Re-evaluating Fundamental Approaches
abstract: Contemporary advancements in natural language processing often rely on expansive, computationally intensive models that utilize extensive general-domain text data via self-supervised pre-training. The substantial operational costs associated with deploying such models in downstream applications have prompted the development of various model compression techniques for these pre-trained representations. However, a straightforward approach—simply pre-training and subsequently fine-tuning compact architectures—has been remarkably overlooked. This investigation initially demonstrates that pre-training maintains its significance even for smaller neural networks, and that fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can achieve performance comparable to more intricate methodologies presented in concurrent research. Building upon these pre-trained compact architectures, we proceed to investigate the transfer of task-specific knowledge from larger, fine-tuned models by employing conventional knowledge distillation. This methodology, which is both simple and broadly applicable, yields additional performance gains. Furthermore, our comprehensive experimental regimen explores the interplay between pre-training and distillation, specifically addressing two variables—model size and characteristics of unlabeled task data—that have received limited scrutiny. A noteworthy finding is that these two processes exhibit a synergistic effect, even when they are applied sequentially to identical datasets. To foster future advancements in this domain, a collection of 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models will be made publicly accessible.

author: Parsons
title: Enhancing Dense Retrieval Models Through Curriculum-Guided Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Prior studies indicate that effective dense retrieval models emerge from distilling ranking knowledge from an existing re-ranking model. We introduce a generic optimization framework leveraging curriculum learning to manage the difficulty of training data derived from the re-ranking (teacher) model. This approach iteratively refines the dense retrieval (student) model, escalating the challenge of the knowledge distillation data presented. It initially feeds the student model coarse preference pairs from the teacher's rankings, then progresses to finer-grained pairwise document ordering demands. Our experimental setup involved a direct implementation of this framework for improving two cutting-edge dense retrieval models. Evaluations on three public passage retrieval datasets confirm the approach's effectiveness.

author: Perez
title: Enhanced Multi-Task Learning for Natural Language Understanding via Distillation and Annealing
abstract: Developing multi-task neural networks capable of surpassing or equaling their single-task counterparts often proves difficult. Our proposed solution involves knowledge distillation, with single-task models instructing a multi-task architecture. An enhancement is a novel technique progressively shifting learning from distillation to supervised learning, enabling the multi-task model to surpass its single-task teachers. Our approach was assessed through multi-task fine-tuning of BERT on the GLUE benchmark. The technique consistently outperforms standard single-task and multi-task training methods.

author: Stewart
title: Achieving Private Deep Learning Model Compression Through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Intelligent mobile applications increasingly demand the deployment of powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) on edge devices. However, the remarkable performance of DNNs typically stems from increasingly intricate models, leading to computational expenses that far exceed the capabilities of mobile hardware. Furthermore, service providers for these applications must gather and utilize extensive volumes of sensitive user data to construct these sophisticated DNN models. Directly placing such models onto public mobile devices introduces an unacceptable privacy risk. To enable the advantages of on-device deep learning while mitigating both capacity and privacy concerns, a novel private model compression framework is introduced. This framework adheres to the knowledge distillation paradigm, integrating hint learning, distillation learning, and self-learning for the development of a compact and rapid neural network. Knowledge transferred from the larger, original model undergoes adaptive bounding and deliberate perturbation to ensure differential privacy. Additionally, an innovative query sample selection technique is presented to decrease the number of queries and manage privacy loss effectively. Comprehensive empirical assessments and a deployment on an Android mobile device confirm that the proposed method not only achieves efficient compression of large models but also delivers a robust privacy guarantee. For instance, on the SVHN dataset, guaranteeing a meaningful (9.83, 10^-6)-differential privacy, the compact model produced by this approach attains a 20-fold compression ratio and a 19-fold speed increase with a minimal accuracy degradation of merely 0.97%.

author: Adams
title: An Empirical Examination of the Claimed Incompatibility between Label Smoothing and Knowledge Distillation
abstract: This study empirically addresses the current assertion that label smoothing and knowledge distillation are fundamentally incompatible. We first posit that this perceived conflict stems from label smoothing eroding relative information within teacher logits. A novel connection is presented on label smoothing's effect on semantically similar and dissimilar class distributions. We then propose a metric to quantitatively assess erased information in sample representations. The viewpoint's one-sidedness and imperfections are then scrutinized through extensive analyses, visualizations, and comprehensive experiments across Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Our findings conclude by outlining specific conditions where label smoothing indeed becomes ineffective.

author: Clark
title: An Examination of Knowledge Distillation's Utility for Federated Learning Across Diverse Model Architectures
abstract: Consider the challenge of developing a universal application programming interface to facilitate federated learning, enabling collaboration among arbitrary collections of data-holding agents. This kind of interface must inherently lack assumptions regarding the specific model architectures employed by participating agents, and it likewise cannot depend on the availability of representative public datasets. Consequently, knowledge distillation stands out as the natural methodology for constructing such communication protocols. Nonetheless, our investigation surprisingly reveals that the majority of straightforward federated learning protocols utilizing knowledge distillation exhibit suboptimal performance. In order to delve into this phenomenon, a novel theoretical framework, referred to as Federated Kernel ridge regression, is introduced, capable of encompassing both disparate model configurations and varied data distributions. The resultant analysis demonstrates that this performance reduction primarily stems from an inherent constraint of knowledge distillation when confronted with heterogeneous data. Our framework's validity is further established through the analysis and subsequent development of additional knowledge distillation-centric protocols. Although their outcomes in practical experiments employing neural networks remain suboptimal, they nonetheless align closely with our theoretical forecasts.

author: Hahn
title: A Unified Knowledge Distillation Approach for Object Detectors Leveraging Pearson Correlation Coefficient
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a prevalent method for training more compact object detection models. Nevertheless, effective distillation between heterogeneous detectors remains an under-explored area. Our investigation empirically reveals that even when detection heads and label assignments differ, superior FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher can still enhance student performance. Directly aligning feature maps for detector distillation, however, presents two key challenges. First, substantial differences in feature magnitude between the teacher and student models can impose excessively strict regularization on the student. Second, FPN stages and channels in the teacher with high feature magnitude might disproportionately influence the distillation loss gradient, thereby overshadowing the contributions of other features in KD and injecting considerable noise. To mitigate these issues, we propose a novel approach that imitates features using the Pearson Correlation Coefficient. This technique shifts the focus to the teacher's relational information and simultaneously relaxes restrictions on feature magnitudes. The method we introduce consistently surpasses established detection KD techniques and is effective across both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairings. Additionally, it exhibits quicker convergence. For example, employing a potent MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, RetinaNet and FCOS, both built on ResNet-50, attain 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, representing gains of 4.1% and 4.8% over baseline performance, respectively.

author: Walter
title: Effective Knowledge Transfer from Advanced Teacher Architectures
abstract: Many existing knowledge distillation approaches concentrate on standard configurations, where teacher models and their associated training methodologies lack the robustness and competitive edge found in state-of-the-art systems. To address this, we propose a novel technique, referred to here as the proposed method, to facilitate superior distillation from a more powerful teacher. Empirical observations indicate that a significant divergence often arises between the predictions of a student and a more proficient teacher. This heightened disparity can disrupt training and diminish the performance of conventional methods that rely on precise prediction alignment, such as through KL divergence. Our research demonstrates that merely maintaining the relationships among the predictions of the teacher and student is adequate. Consequently, we introduce a loss function, based on correlation, which explicitly captures the inherent inter-class relationships encoded by the teacher model. Furthermore, recognizing that individual instances exhibit varying semantic similarities to different classes, this relational matching principle is broadened to encompass the intra-class domain. The proposed approach is straightforward while remaining highly practical. Comprehensive experimental evaluations confirm its excellent adaptability across diverse architectural configurations, model capacities, and training paradigms. It consistently yields state-of-the-art results in tasks such as image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation.

author: Edwards
title: Privacy-Enhanced Federated Learning through Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
abstract: A machine learning paradigm, Federated Learning (FL), involves multiple local entities cooperatively developing a central model without centralizing their training datasets. Standard FL strategies, often encompassing parameter sharing or co-distillation, aim to address challenges posed by non-IID data distribution. These methods, however, frequently face substantial communication limitations. Crucially, the potential for sensitive data leakage is also present. Our work introduces a communication-efficient and privacy-conscious approach within a FL setting. This method leverages one-shot offline knowledge distillation, utilizing publicly accessible, unlabeled data across diverse domains. We propose a quantized and noisy aggregation of predictions from fully trained local models, providing robust privacy assurances without compromising model accuracy. Comprehensive evaluations on image and text classification tasks demonstrate that our privacy-preserving technique outperforms conventional FL baselines, showing improved performance in both classification accuracy and communication efficiency.

author: Rios
title: Enhancing Neural Topic Model Performance via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Large document collections frequently employ topic models for extracting human-understandable themes, thereby facilitating comprehension. A synthesis of desirable traits, originating from probabilistic topic models and from pretrained transformers, is achieved through knowledge distillation. The proposed method exhibits modularity and can be readily applied to any neural topic model to elevate topic quality. We substantiate this through its application to two models possessing distinct architectures, achieving state-of-the-art topic coherence. Furthermore, the flexible framework demonstrates improved performance, not merely in the overall aggregate of all derived topics (a common metric), but critically also through direct head-to-head comparisons of corresponding topics.

author: Foster
title: Optimizing Click-Through Rate Prediction via Ensemble Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deep learning architectures have recently garnered significant attention for click-through rate (CTR) prediction, yielding improved accuracy in various industrial settings. Nevertheless, current efforts primarily concentrate on developing intricate network designs to better capture complex feature interactions and dynamic user behaviors. The resulting heightened model complexity can impede online inference speed, thereby limiting real-time application deployment. In contrast, this study explores a novel model training approach centered on knowledge distillation (KD). KD functions as a teacher-student framework, facilitating the transfer of acquired knowledge from a more powerful teacher model to a simpler student model. This KD-driven method not only enables the simplification of the student model to a standard deep neural network (DNN) but also achieves substantial accuracy gains over current state-of-the-art teacher models. These observed benefits motivated further investigation into employing a robust ensemble of teachers to achieve even more precise student model training. Furthermore, we introduce novel techniques designed to improve ensembled CTR prediction, specifically teacher gating and early stopping based on distillation loss. Extensive experiments were conducted, comparing our method against twelve existing models across three distinct industrial datasets. Both offline and online A/B testing outcomes consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of our knowledge distillation-centric training paradigm.

author: Rocha
title: Inter-Layer Knowledge Transfer for Few-Shot Network Compression
abstract: Shrinking deep neural networks to produce more compact models is a frequently employed technique. However, the majority of established compression approaches demand substantial training datasets for fine-tuning to preserve performance, a requirement that often conflicts with privacy and security considerations. To balance privacy and model efficacy, this research examines network compression under few-shot conditions, specifically addressing how to efficiently reduce network size with minimal performance degradation when only a handful of examples are available per category. A central difficulty in low-data network compression stems from substantial inference-time estimation errors generated by the original network, given that the reduced network readily overfits the scarce training data. Such estimation inaccuracies are likely to spread and intensify across individual layers, ultimately impairing the final network output. Our approach tackles this issue by introducing a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation method. By connecting corresponding hidden layers of the teacher and student networks, errors accumulating layer by layer are effectively curtailed. The presented framework is broadly applicable, integrating seamlessly with existing network compression techniques, for instance, pruning. Results from numerous experiments on widely used benchmark datasets reveal that this layer-wise knowledge transfer mechanism significantly enhances student network accuracy, particularly when training instances are scarce.

author: Ellis
title: Investigating Representation-Focused Knowledge Distillation within Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Knowledge distillation serves as a learning strategy to enhance resource-constrained graph neural networks (GNNs) employing powerful, often unwieldy, teacher models. Prior GNN distillation efforts introduced a local structure preserving loss, aligning edge-defined local structural relationships between student and teacher's learned node embeddings. Our investigation probes whether maintaining the teacher's global topological embedding of graph data constitutes a superior distillation objective for GNNs, given frequent latent relationships and noisy connections within real-world graphs. We introduce a contrastive representation distillation method. This technique employs contrastive learning for implicit global topology retention, aligning student node embeddings with teacher representations in a shared space. An expanded set of benchmarks is also provided, featuring large-scale real-world datasets where teacher-student GNN performance disparity is substantial. Across four datasets and fourteen diverse GNN architectures, our method consistently enhances lightweight GNN performance and robustness, surpassing the local structure preserving method (and its global variant), plus 2D computer vision baselines. Representational similarity analysis between teacher and student embedding fields indicates our approach balances the preservation of local and global relationships, unlike other structure-preserving methods that prioritize one. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns.

author: Baker
title: Optimizing Non-Autoregressive Translation for Infrequent Vocabulary: Leveraging Parallel Data More Effectively
abstract:
Synthetic data for non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models is frequently generated using knowledge distillation (KD) techniques. A notable disparity, however, arises concerning low-frequency vocabulary when comparing distilled data with its source, which consequently results in elevated error rates for such word predictions. Our approach mitigates this issue by integrating raw data directly into NAT models via a pretraining phase. Investigations into directed alignments revealed that while KD promotes a more deterministic linkage of low-frequency source words to their target counterparts, it proves inadequate in establishing a sufficient number of alignments from low-frequency target words back to the source. Consequently, a novel method termed reverse KD is introduced to foster a greater quantity of alignments involving low-frequency words from the target language. A novel training regimen is formulated by integrating these complementary techniques, thereby fully leveraging both authentic and synthetic datasets to further enhance NAT performance. Experiments were performed utilizing five distinct translation benchmarks across a pair of advanced architectural designs. The findings indicate that the methodology introduced consistently and substantially elevates translation quality, achieved through a reduction in errors pertaining to low-frequency terms. Notably, this method attained BLEU scores of 28.2 for the WMT14 English-German dataset and 33.9 for the WMT16 Romanian-English dataset, respectively. The associated code, datasets, and pretrained models are accessible online at 
https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT.

author: Wright
title: Semantic Knowledge Distillation Facilitating Thorough Video Scene Comprehension
abstract: Complete environmental comprehension is critically important for autonomous systems. Prior investigations have demonstrated that deep neural networks are capable of acquiring knowledge of both geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) directly from single-camera video input. This learning occurs without the need for explicit ground truth supervision, which is notably challenging to obtain for these specific problems. This work advances holistic scene interpretation using monocular cameras by simultaneously learning depth, motion, and semantic information. The semantic supervision is derived from a pre-trained network that distills proxy ground truth images. Our approach tackles these three interdependent tasks concurrently through two primary mechanisms: first, an innovative training scheme integrating both knowledge distillation and self-supervision; second, a streamlined network architecture that facilitates effective scene comprehension on both high-power GPUs and resource-constrained embedded devices. We comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method and confirm its attainment of state-of-the-art performance in monocular depth estimation, optical flow, and motion segmentation.

author: Hoffman
title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Communication efficiency is a critical concern in distributed learning frameworks, where exchanging model parameters, such as gradients or weights in federated learning setups, often supplants direct data sharing across workers. This approach, while common, becomes prohibitively costly for modern deep neural networks, given their extensive parameter counts and limited communication resources. In this context, a powerful alternative is federated distillation (FD), a distributed learning technique that exclusively transmits model outputs. The dimensionality of these outputs is typically significantly smaller than the full model sizes; for example, the MNIST dataset involves merely 10 labels. This chapter aims to thoroughly elucidate FD's principles, illustrating its robust communication efficiency and its broad applicability across diverse tasks. To achieve this, the exposition is structured into three main segments. Initially, to clarify the fundamental operational mechanisms of FD, a novel asymptotic analysis is presented for two foundational algorithms: knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD). This analysis leverages the theoretical framework of the neural tangent kernel (NTK). Subsequent sections detail a baseline implementation of this distillation method, focusing on a classification task. Its performance, encompassing both accuracy and communication efficiency, is then contrasted with federated learning (FL). The final part demonstrates the versatility of this approach across various distributed learning scenarios and environments, specifically exploring two selected applications: its use over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and its application in reinforcement learning contexts.

author: Baker
title: Integrating Dissimilar Classifiers through Distillation
abstract: This research addresses the challenge of combining insights from multiple classification models, each possessing distinct architectures and operating on varying target classes, into a singular classifier. This process relies solely on an available collection of generic unlabelled data. The specific issue explored involves consolidating varied classification models. Such a situation arises when information originates from numerous sources, yet data exchange among them is restricted, for instance, by privacy regulations, permitting only the distribution of individually trained models. Furthermore, individual sources might lack sufficient data to train across all classes or possess inadequate computational resources to implement identical classification models. To resolve this, a generalized form of knowledge distillation is introduced for merging these heterogeneous classifiers. A probabilistic relationship is established that connects the outputs from these diverse classifiers with the overall probability distribution across all possible classes. From this derived relationship, two categories of approaches are put forth: one built upon cross-entropy minimisation and another utilizing matrix factorisation. These techniques enable the estimation of soft labels for all classes using unlabelled samples. These estimated soft labels then serve as substitutes for ground truth labels during the training of a consolidated classifier. Comprehensive empirical evaluations, conducted on the ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets, demonstrate that the proposed methods markedly surpass a straightforward adaptation of distillation. Our approaches nearly match the accuracy performance of classifiers trained centrally under supervised conditions.

author: Richards
title: A Framework for Text Generation Integrating Knowledge Distillation with Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: The discrete nature of textual data significantly impedes generative adversarial networks in natural language processing applications. Conversely, GANs have achieved substantial success in computer vision, producing high-fidelity images. Nevertheless, developing robust text generation is a critical goal for many NLP domains, such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. To mitigate these challenges, this study presents a method employing knowledge distillation to adapt the GAN framework for text generation. We demonstrate that autoencoders yield a continuous representation for sentences. This representation is smooth, assigning non-zero probabilities to several words. Its properties are then distilled, guiding the generator to create analogous smooth embeddings. Experiments across diverse datasets confirm our method's efficacy. Our methodology outperforms traditional GAN-based text generation without pre-training, measured by BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD).

author: Hurst
title: Knowledge Distillation for Compact, High-Performance Ranking Models in Recommender Systems
abstract: Developing effective and efficient ranking models for recommender systems is crucial. Knowledge distillation (KD) has successfully enhanced both efficiency and effectiveness within image recognition tasks. Herein, a knowledge distillation approach is introduced, specifically tailored for learning-to-rank challenges. This approach instructs a more compact student model to order documents/items, utilizing training data and supervisory signals from an extensive teacher model. The student model yields ranking performance equivalent to the extensive teacher model, while its reduced footprint ensures more efficient online inference. The method demonstrates flexibility, being agnostic to the specific ranking model architectures used for the teacher or student. We also address inherent challenges of distillation in ranking. Experimental results, leveraging public datasets and state-of-the-art recommendation models, confirmed the approach's objectives. The student model, trained using this method, achieved a model footprint under half that of the teacher, while attaining ranking performance comparable to the teacher model and substantially outperforming a student model trained conventionally.

author: Ross
title: Enhancing Neural Machine Translation through Ensemble Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Student networks can achieve enhanced performance by absorbing knowledge from a more capable teacher network, a process known as knowledge distillation. The translation of sentences using Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engines is computationally demanding, and employing a more compact model reduces this processing time. This work demonstrates a procedure to impart the translation proficiency from both an ensemble teacher and an oracle BLEU teacher network onto a singular NMT system. Moreover, improvements in translation are achieved using a teacher network possessing the identical architecture and dimensions as its student counterpart. Given that student model training remains resource-intensive, we introduce a novel data subset selection technique, informed by the teacher model's understanding, which not only accelerates the training phase but also yields superior translation performance. The proposed methodologies require no modifications to the codebase and are readily implementable across any NMT architecture, thereby facilitating faster decoding.

author: Robinson
title: Investigating and Refining Lexical Selection within Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: Training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models critically relies on knowledge distillation (KD), which simplifies the inherent data complexity from raw input using an autoregressive teacher model. Our empirical investigation reveals that this training methodology inadvertently results in the transmission of lexical choice inaccuracies for infrequently occurring terms from the teacher to the NAT model. To mitigate this challenge, our proposed method involves exposing raw data to NAT models, aiming to reinstate crucial insights about rare words that are absent in the distilled training material. For this purpose, we integrate an auxiliary Kullback-Leibler divergence component that evaluates the NAT model's word selection against what is present in the raw data. Findings from experiments conducted across various language pairs and model architectures unequivocally attest to the efficacy and broad applicability of the proposed method. Comprehensive analyses further corroborate the assertion that performance enhancements are indeed attributable to mitigating the lexical choice inaccuracies concerning low-frequency vocabulary, facilitated by our method. Notably, our method advances the state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance for NAT on the WMT14 English-German dataset to 27.8 BLEU points and on the WMT16 Romanian-English dataset to 33.8 BLEU points. The corresponding source code will be made publicly available.

author: Bright
title: Enabling Real-World Lipreading Through Model Distillation and Efficiency Improvements
abstract: Lipreading capabilities have improved substantially thanks to advancements in neural networks. While recent studies have concentrated on enhancing performance through optimal architectures or improving generalization, a considerable disparity persists between existing methodologies and the necessities for successful deployment of lipreading in real-world scenarios. This investigation introduces several innovations designed to substantially narrow this gap. First, performance is significantly elevated on LRW and LRW-1000 datasets, reaching new state-of-the-art figures of 88.5% and 46.6% respectively, achieved through the application of self-distillation. Secondly, a series of architectural modifications are presented, including an innovative Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head. These modifications drastically reduce the computational expense, bringing it down to a small fraction of the processing demands of even prior efficient models. Thirdly, the utility of knowledge distillation for restoring performance in lightweight models is demonstrated. This process yields a spectrum of models exhibiting varied trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency. Notably, the most effective of our lightweight models reach performance levels equivalent to the prevailing state-of-the-art, concurrently exhibiting an 8.2x cut in computational cost and a 3.9x drop in parameter count. This breakthrough is anticipated to facilitate the integration of lipreading solutions into practical applications.

author: Hicks
title: Knowledge Distillation for Adaptive Model Training
abstract: The necessity of domain adaptation arises frequently in real-world contexts, as the statistical properties of training data often diverge from those of test data. Existing Deep Learning methods designed for domain adaptation typically necessitate co-training across source and target domain data, which presents challenges. This requirement renders them less effective in situations demanding adaptation to numerous domains or in cases of continuously evolving domains, like spam filtering where attackers frequently alter their techniques. To address this limitation, we introduce a new methodology that generalizes Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) specifically for domain adaptation tasks. A student model achieves a state-of-the-art level for unsupervised domain adaptation, utilizing multiple sources, as demonstrated on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark. This is accomplished by considering the domain-specific expertise of several teachers and the commonalities between their domains. When acquiring knowledge from one teacher, relying solely on domain similarity proves inadequate for assessing trustworthiness. To address this, we introduce an uncomplicated metric exhibiting strong correlation with the teacher's target domain accuracy. Our findings confirm that the inclusion of high-confidence examples, identified through this metric, allows the student model to attain state-of-the-art results within the single-source context.

author: Williams
title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation via Adversarial Sample Generation
abstract: In contemporary deep learning, transferring knowledge from a large teacher network to a smaller student model presents a widespread challenge. Access to the original data used for training the teacher is often restricted, a situation amplified by expanding dataset sizes and strict privacy mandates. We introduce a novel methodology to train a student that mirrors its teacher's predictions, completely omitting any training data or associated metadata. This is accomplished by leveraging an adversarial generator, which actively seeks input examples where the student's output deviates substantially from the teacher's; these identified examples then refine the student. Our student model closely mirrors its teacher's performance on uncomplicated datasets such as SVHN. For CIFAR10, our data-free approach surpasses current state-of-the-art performance in few-shot distillation settings (with 100 images allocated per class), without requiring any actual training data. We also put forth a quantifiable metric evaluating belief congruence between teacher and student, particularly in regions adjacent to decision boundaries. Observations indicate a significantly higher congruence for our zero-shot student with the teacher, compared to a student distilled using real training data. The corresponding source code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

author: Rodriguez
title: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Graph Neural Networks: Surpassing Teacher Performance with Interpretable Student Models
abstract: The domain of machine learning frequently addresses semi-supervised learning tasks on graphs, which represents a critical challenge. Modern classification approaches relying on graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently demonstrated superior performance compared to conventional techniques, for instance, label propagation. Nevertheless, the intricate designs inherent in these neural architectures generate an involved prediction process, failing to fully utilize valuable domain-specific information present within the data, such as the expectation that structurally linked nodes often share identical classes. To resolve these aforementioned challenges, this work introduces a framework grounded in knowledge distillation. This framework acquires the expertise from any pre-trained GNN model, designated as a teacher, subsequently transferring it into a meticulously constructed student model. The student model incorporates two straightforward predictive mechanisms, specifically label propagation and feature transformation, each inherently maintaining prior knowledge based on graph structure and node features, in that order. More precisely, the student model's architecture is conceived as a learnable amalgamation of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. Consequently, the resulting student model capitalizes on both the inherent prior knowledge and the transferred expertise from GNN teachers, leading to enhanced predictive performance. Additionally, the prediction procedure implemented by the trained student model exhibits greater interpretability compared to that of GNNs. Evaluations were conducted across five widely available benchmark datasets. Seven distinct GNN models, comprising GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII, and GLP, served as teacher models throughout these experiments. Empirical findings consistently reveal that the developed student model surpasses its respective teacher model, demonstrating an average performance improvement ranging from 1.4% to 4.7%. The associated source code and experimental data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF.

author: Burton
title: Accelerating Large-Scale Transformer Language Models via Hardware-Aware Block-Structured Pruning
abstract: Despite their high accuracy in many natural language processing tasks, pre-trained large-scale language models encounter significant hardware limitations, especially regarding weight storage and computational speed, hindering their adoption in edge computing. This work presents an efficient method for transformer-based large-scale language representation using block-structured pruning, specifically designed to be hardware-friendly. Optimization relies on the integration of reweighted group Lasso, which is applied within the block-structured pruning framework. This approach yields substantial reductions in weight storage and computation while achieving high compression rates. Experiments on BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT across General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show compression up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain tasks. The proposed method also proves orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models like DistilBERT, which use knowledge distillation. When applied to DistilBERT, an additional average compression of 1.79x is achieved, again with zero or minor accuracy degradation. The final compressed models are therefore well-suited for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.

author: Conner
title: Knowledge Transfer from BERT to Uncomplicated Neural Architectures for Specific Tasks
abstract: The field of natural language processing has seen a continuous trend towards more intricate and profound neural network models. Exemplifying this trajectory are recent deep language representation models, such as BERT, ELMo, and GPT. Consequently, the prevailing view suggests that prior generations of shallower neural networks for language understanding are no longer viable. Nevertheless, this study illustrates that basic, low-complexity neural networks retain their capacity for competitive performance, requiring no architectural modifications, supplementary training data, or extra input features. We introduce a strategy for transferring knowledge from BERT, which stands as a cutting-edge language representation model, into a unilayer BiLSTM and its siamese variant designed for tasks involving pairs of sentences. Utilizing various datasets encompassing paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, our approach yields performance akin to ELMo, all while consuming approximately 100-fold fewer parameters and demanding 15-fold reduced inference time.

author: Henderson
title: Knowledge Distillation for Graph-Independent Node Classification with Multi-layer Perceptrons
abstract: While Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel in graph machine learning, demonstrating strong results in wide node classification tasks, their practical deployment in industrial settings is hindered by scalability issues. These issues arise from their inherent data dependency, where GNN inference requires fetching neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, imposing substantial latency burdens on time-critical applications. Existing methods for accelerating GNN inference, such as pruning and quantization, reduce Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations; however, their improvements are limited since they do not resolve the fundamental data dependency. Multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), conversely, inherently possess no graph dependency and perform inference significantly faster than GNNs, though they generally offer lower accuracy for node classification. Inspired by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we unite GNNs and MLPs via knowledge distillation (KD). Our investigation reveals that the performance of MLPs can be substantially enhanced through GNN-based knowledge distillation. The resulting distilled MLPs operate without inference graph dependency. We demonstrate that these distilled MLPs, while achieving competitive accuracy, infer 146X to 273X faster than GNNs and 14X to 27X faster than alternative acceleration methods. Within a production context involving both transductive and inductive predictions over seven datasets, the distilled MLPs show an average 12.36% accuracy improvement over stand-alone MLPs, matching GNN performance on six out of seven datasets. A comprehensive analysis elucidates the conditions under which these distilled MLPs achieve accuracies comparable to GNNs, suggesting their utility as a practical choice for latency-constrained systems.

author: Brown
title: Comprehensive Compression for Visual Transformers
abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have recently seen a surge in popularity. Despite their lack of specialized image operators like convolutions, ViTs deliver competitive performance when adequately trained on extensive data. However, their significant computational burden persists, primarily due to the intricate stacking of multi-head self-attention modules. While convolutional neural network compression is a well-established field with extensive literature, the area of Vision Transformer compression is still nascent, with current studies often addressing only one or two compression dimensions. This paper introduces an integrated ViT compression methodology, which proficiently combines three effective strategies: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We propose an end-to-end, budget-constrained optimization framework designed to simultaneously learn model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios and masks, and skip configurations, all under the guidance of a distillation loss. The primal-dual algorithm is utilized to solve this optimization problem. Experimental results on the ImageNet dataset, using ViT variants such as DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones, consistently show the proposed method outperforms recent benchmarks. For instance, DeiT-Tiny's FLOPs can be reduced by 50% with almost no corresponding accuracy decline. The source code is publicly available online.

author: James
title: Achieving Robust Cross-Modal Representations via Iterative Self-Distillation
abstract: Web-mined image captioning datasets contain noisy many-to-many correspondences that CLIP's vision-language learning objective fails to adequately handle. Consequently, this leads to compute and data inefficiencies. To tackle this issue, we present a novel cross-modal contrastive learning framework. It applies iterative self-distillation and gentle image-text alignments to acquire robust representations efficiently from noisy data. The proposed model distills its internal knowledge to dynamically create soft-alignment targets for a portion of images and captions within each minibatch, subsequently updating its parameters. Evaluations across 14 benchmark datasets affirm that our methodology consistently outperforms CLIP in several settings, specifically for image-text retrieval, zero-shot classification, and linear probe transfer, without incurring additional computational expenses. An ImageNet-based robustness test-bed analysis demonstrates that the technique achieves superior effective robustness against natural distribution shifts, relative to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP. Finally, pretraining datasets whose sizes vary by two orders of magnitude reveals that performance gains over CLIP typically scale with the volume of training examples.

author: Ferrell
title: Optimizing Supernet Training with Adaptive Alpha-Divergence
abstract: Automated design of efficient neural architectures often leverages weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS), a highly effective approach. This method constructs a supernet comprising all potential architectures as its sub-networks, then performs joint training of both the supernet and its constituent sub-networks. Successful weight-sharing NAS fundamentally depends on effectively transferring knowledge from the supernet to the sub-networks. A critical observation, however, reveals that Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, a commonly employed distillation metric, can result in student sub-networks either exaggerating or diminishing the uncertainty inherent in the teacher supernet, thereby degrading their subsequent performance. To address this, our research introduces an enhanced supernet training methodology utilizing a more generalized alpha-divergence. Through an adaptive selection process of this alpha-divergence, we simultaneously mitigate both the over-estimation and under-estimation of the teacher model's uncertainty. We applied this proposed training strategy, which leverages alpha-divergence, to slimmable neural networks as well as weight-sharing NAS, confirming substantial performance gains. Our method yielded a model family that consistently outperforms prior-art benchmarks such as BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS, across diverse FLOPs levels. An 80.0% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet was achieved with a mere 444M FLOPs. The implementation code and all pretrained models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

author: Rice
title: Improving Fake Media Detection Adaptability Through Continual Representation Learning and Distillation
abstract: Despite significant advancements in artificial intelligence, current systems frequently depend on static datasets within unchanging operational environments. Simultaneously, the proliferation of fake media, encompassing deepfakes and synthetic facial images, presents a critical challenge in modern multimedia technology. While numerous highly accurate deepfake detection methods have been introduced, their performance suffers substantially due to their reliance on predefined datasets and restricted evaluation conditions. This limitation necessitates approaches capable of learning incrementally. Continual learning, an evolving research area, investigates how AI systems can acquire knowledge sequentially from continuous data streams, mirroring biological learning processes. Addressing these challenges, this investigation applies continual learning principles to the dynamics of neural network training, underscoring its potential for substantial improvements in data efficiency. We introduce a novel approach that integrates Continual Learning (CL), Representation Learning (RL), and Knowledge Distillation (KD). This method is engineered to execute sequential domain adaptation tasks for emerging deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets. Within a teacher-student model configuration, it effectively minimizes the phenomenon of catastrophic forgetting. Extensive experimental validation confirms the proposed method's proficiency in domain adaptation for identifying low-quality deepfake videos and GAN-generated images across various datasets, consistently surpassing the performance of existing state-of-the-art baseline techniques.

author: Maddox
title: Compressing BERT Models via Many-to-Many Layer Mapping and Earth Mover's Distance
abstract: The widespread adoption of pre-trained language models like BERT in diverse natural language processing (NLP) tasks is limited by their substantial storage and computational requirements, particularly for deployment on devices with restricted resources. To address this, we introduce a novel BERT distillation approach employing many-to-many layer mapping. This design enables individual intermediate student layers to acquire knowledge from any of the teacher's intermediate layers. Consequently, the resulting model can adaptively draw insights from various teacher layers to suit different NLP tasks. Furthermore, Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) is integrated to quantify the minimum cumulative expenditure necessary for knowledge transfer between the teacher and student networks. EMD proves instrumental for efficient matching within the many-to-many layer mapping scheme, capable of measuring semantic distance effectively even when network layers differ in size. A cost attention mechanism is also presented, designed to automatically determine the layer weights for EMD. This component is anticipated to enhance the model's overall performance and quicken its convergence. Through comprehensive evaluations on the GLUE benchmark, the introduced approach exhibits competitive performance against established alternatives, both in terms of achieved accuracy and the degree of model compression.

author: Valencia
title: A Comprehensive Review of Deep Neural Network Compression in Natural Language Processing
abstract: Significant progress has been observed recently in natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR), primarily driven by advanced deep learning architectures. Notable examples of these include Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs) networks. Furthermore, a range of Transformer [120] based models, such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98], and GShard [63], have also achieved substantial impact. However, the immense scale of these models presents a challenge. Practical applications in real-world scenarios require models with smaller footprints, reduced response times, and lower energy consumption. This review systematically explores six distinct methodologies for shrinking such models: Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, and Sub-quadratic Transformer based methods. The primary objective is to facilitate their integration into actual industrial NLP applications. Recognizing the urgent requirement for developing applications with both efficient and compact models, alongside the significant volume of recent publications in this domain, we contend that this survey effectively structures the extensive research performed by the 'deep learning for NLP' community during recent years, presenting it as an organized narrative.

author: Smith
title: Distillation-Based Automated Search for Generative Adversarial Network Compression
abstract: Compressing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has recently garnered interest. This stems from a heightened need for deploying such models onto mobile equipment, enabling varied applications including image translation, enhancement, and editing. Yet, in contrast to extensive work on compressing other deep models, the field of GAN compression (specifically of generators) is still in its early phases. Current algorithms for GAN compression exhibit limitations, often restricted to particular GAN architectures and losses. Drawing on AutoML's recent accomplishments in deep model compression, we extend its application to GAN compression through a novel framework. Utilizing a custom-designed, efficient search space, our method performs end-to-end discovery of novel efficient generators, subject to specified computational resource constraints. Knowledge distillation from the original GAN model directs this search, thereby achieving the desired compression. This framework operates fully automatically, stands alone (requiring no pre-trained discriminators), and demonstrates generic applicability across diverse GAN models. Its performance is assessed on two typical GAN challenges: image translation and super resolution. Without extensive tuning, the proposed approach generates notably lightweight but highly competitive compressed models, significantly outperforming current alternatives. Source code and pre-trained models are publicly accessible at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

author: Le
title: Enhanced Video-Pose Representations for Understanding Activities of Daily Living
abstract: Recognizing Activities of Daily Living (ADL) frequently demands the modeling of fine-grained details due to their visual similarities. Methodologies combining RGB and 3D Poses are prevalent in this research area, as contemporary 3D ConvNets are too inflexible to adequately capture subtle visual patterns across actions. However, the computation of 3D poses from an RGB stream is resource-intensive when appropriate sensors are unavailable. This limitation constrains the application of such techniques in real-world scenarios requiring low latency. A key question thus arises: what is the optimal strategy for leveraging 3D Poses in ADL recognition? To address this, we present an extension of a pose-driven attention mechanism, specifically the Video-Pose Network (VPN). Our work explores two separate directions: one involves transferring pose knowledge into RGB features using feature-level distillation; the other focuses on emulating pose-driven attention by means of attention-level distillation. These two distinct strategies are then unified into a single model, which we term the developed method. Our findings demonstrate that this developed method is not only effective but also provides significant speed improvements and high robustness against noisy Poses. The proposed approach surpasses representative baselines on four public datasets, irrespective of 3D Poses availability.

author: Maldonado
title: Knowledge Transfer via Feature Replication
abstract: The common approach of knowledge distillation (KD) enables the training of efficient "student" networks by leveraging high-capacity "teacher" networks. Typically, conventional methods rely on the soft logits generated by the teacher as supplementary supervision during student network training. This investigation asserts that a more beneficial strategy involves guiding the student to replicate the teacher's features within the penultimate layer. This not only allows the student to directly acquire more potent information from the teacher's features, but feature replication is also viable for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Empirical results demonstrate that this technique achieves superior accuracy compared to traditional KD. To further enhance feature replication, a feature vector is disaggregated into its magnitude and directional components. We contend that the teacher should provide greater flexibility regarding the student feature's magnitude, while the student should concentrate more intensely on mimicking the feature direction. Addressing this requirement, a unique loss function is introduced, which is predicated on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). Aided by this new loss, the proposed method effectively replicates feature directions with higher fidelity, eases restrictions on feature magnitudes, and attains cutting-edge distillation accuracy. We offer theoretical examinations explaining LSH's role in facilitating feature direction replication, and additionally expand feature replication's applicability to multi-label recognition and object detection.

author: Herrera
title: Parameter Reduction for Generative Adversarial Networks via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks find utility across diverse machine learning applications, including domain transfer, super resolution, and generating synthetic data. However, modern state-of-the-art GANs typically incorporate tens of millions of parameters, which presents significant obstacles for deployment in resource-constrained environments like low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware (e.g., mobile devices) or for tasks demanding real-time processing. To date, research on methods for reducing the parameter count in GAN architectures is notably absent. Consequently, a novel approach is introduced for GAN compression, leveraging knowledge distillation principles. This involves a more compact "student" GAN learning to replicate the behavior of a larger "teacher" GAN. Our experimental results demonstrate that the application of these distillation techniques to teacher GANs, specifically on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets, yields compression ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, in sequence, without compromising the output image quality. Empirical findings also indicate a qualitative ceiling for the extent of GAN compression. Furthermore, when comparing models within an identical parameter budget, GANs subjected to our proposed method exhibit superior performance compared to those trained via conventional approaches. This enhanced performance is posited to stem partly from the beneficial optimization landscape characteristic of over-parameterized GANs, which facilitates effective training through alternating gradient descent. Therefore, the strategy of initially training an over-parameterized GAN and subsequently applying our developed compression scheme results in a high-fidelity generative model characterized by a reduced parameter count.

author: Davidson
title: Enhanced Re-Identification Robustness through Multi-View Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Re-Identification performance often suffers significant decline when query inputs are limited to single images, such as in the Image-To-Video scenario, despite standard methods achieving robustness by integrating tracking information in a Video-To-Video manner. Earlier research has attempted to mitigate this severe performance degradation by transferring temporal cues from video-based networks to image-based ones. This paper introduces a novel training paradigm designed to facilitate the transfer of superior knowledge derived from a collection of perspectives depicting the same target object. Our knowledge distillation approach utilizes this rich visual diversity as a supervisory signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher network processes a broader array of views to guide a student network that operates with fewer views. Consequently, the student network not only surpasses its teacher's performance but also establishes a new state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video re-identification, demonstrating substantial improvements: 6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId, and 5% on VeRi-776. A comprehensive investigation, spanning Person, Vehicle, and Animal Re-ID tasks, provides both qualitative and quantitative insights into the properties of the proposed method. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

author: Rodriguez
title: Securing Graph Neural Network Release Through Differential Privacy
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are gaining prominence in sensitive areas like healthcare, raising privacy questions about trained GNNs. They notably exhibit vulnerability to attacks such as membership inference, even under black-box access. A novel privacy-preserving system is presented for centralized GNN model dissemination. It facilitates GNN release, trained on public data yet incorporating private knowledge, leveraging an available public unlabeled graph while ensuring privacy. The system merges knowledge distillation with two noise mechanisms: random subsampling and noisy labeling, achieving rigorous privacy guarantees. Its theoretical underpinnings are analyzed using Renyi differential privacy. Our empirical findings demonstrate strong efficacy relative to several baselines suitable for graph-structured data. The implementation's software is openly shared.

author: Graham
title: A Regularization Strategy Employing Multi-Level Branching for Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning faces a critical challenge from client data heterogeneity and imbalance, which causes inconsistencies in local networks and compromises global model convergence stability. To alleviate these limitations, a novel architectural regularization technique is proposed. It constructs, within each local model, multiple auxiliary branches by grafting local and global subnetworks at various levels. Moreover, representations from the local model's main pathway are made congruent with those from the auxiliary hybrid pathways through online knowledge distillation. The method proves effective at robustifying the global model even in non-IID settings and integrates conveniently into various federated learning frameworks without incurring additional communication costs. Comprehensive empirical studies demonstrate remarkable performance gains in accuracy and efficiency relative to existing methods. Access to the implementation's source code is provided on our dedicated project page.

author: Chavez
title: Training Data-Independent Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Progress in model compression has yielded techniques for reducing the footprint of extensive neural networks substantially, typically while preserving nearly all accuracy. Yet, these strategies invariably necessitate the initial training data. This dependency becomes problematic when networks are developed on extremely large datasets, or when data distribution is restricted due to privacy implications or security risks, such as in biometrics applications. We introduce an approach for knowledge distillation that requires no training data. This method facilitates the compression of deep neural networks, even those trained on vast datasets, by exclusively utilizing additional metadata included with a released pretrained model. Furthermore, we investigate diverse forms of metadata applicable to the proposed technique and examine the compromises associated with each.

author: Mckay
title: Boosting Efficiency in Large-scale Language Model Distillation with Mixup
abstract: Despite recent impressive empirical performance shown by large-scale language models, their substantial size, elevated power consumption, and diminished inference speeds significantly impede their application on memory- and computation-constrained platforms. A well-established method for compressing such large models is knowledge distillation (KD). However, the application of KD faces obstacles. Foremost, extensive neural networks commonly memorize training instances, resulting in predictions that are inconsistent when the data distribution experiences even slight shifts. Additionally, student models obtain limited chances to acquire valuable information from their teacher when specific task-related data is sparse. To tackle these challenges, the current investigation presents a data-agnostic distillation framework. This method harnesses mixup, an uncomplicated but effective data augmentation procedure, to instill superior generalization capabilities in the derived model. The student is directed to mirror the teacher's output. This applies to both the original data points and synthetic instances created by linear interpolation of example pairs. From a theoretical viewpoint, it is proven that, under appropriate conditions, the presented methodology results in a diminished difference between generalization error and empirical error. Investigations were conducted on the GLUE benchmark to validate its efficacy. This approach consistently achieves substantial performance improvements beyond standard KD training and outperforms several competitive baselines. The benefits of the proposed method are further substantiated by trials undertaken in a limited-data environment and by exhaustive ablation analyses.

author: Liu
title: Enabling Multimodal Generative Capabilities in CLIP through Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Dual-stream architectures, exemplified by CLIP, have shown remarkable effectiveness in diverse multimodal alignment tasks, a consequence of extensive vision-language pre-training (VLP) utilizing vast collections of image-text pairs. Despite this success, these models lack the capacity for multimodal generative operations, primarily due to the inherent weakness of their text encoder. To overcome this limitation, our method proposes an enhancement for the dual-stream VLP architecture: integrating a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD). This integration grants the model multimodal generation capability. The proposed VLKD approach offers significant efficiency, both in terms of data requirements and computational overhead, when compared to training a model from scratch. Empirical findings demonstrate that the resulting model achieves robust zero-shot performance across various multimodal generation tasks, including open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For instance, it attains a zero-shot accuracy of 44.5% on the VQAv2 dataset. This performance surpasses that of the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model, despite employing seven times fewer parameters. Moreover, the PLM's fundamental abilities in textual comprehension and generation are fully preserved after the VLKD process. This characteristic ensures the model's versatility, making it suitable for both multimodal and unimodal applications.

author: Mason
title: Feature Embedding for Compact Network Training
abstract: Though extensively applied, deep convolutional neural networks demand significant storage and computational resources, hindering mobile device deployment. Knowledge distillation seeks to optimize portable student networks by transferring expertise from large, pre-trained teacher networks. Conventional teacher-student methods commonly employ auxiliary fully-connected layers to link intermediate network layers, introducing many additional parameters. Our technique, conversely, propagates teacher information to the student without adding new optimizable variables. The teacher-student paradigm is re-envisioned from a novel feature embedding perspective. Incorporating a locality preserving loss guides the student network to produce low-dimensional features, ensuring these features capture the intrinsic characteristics of their high-dimensional counterparts from the teacher network. Consequently, the derived compact network inherently sustains performance comparable to the teacher network. A theoretical analysis substantiates the proposed method's reduced computational complexity. Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets and trained networks show our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in computational and storage efficiency.

author: White
title: Generating Translated Images with Compact Adversarial Networks Through Distillation
abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are extensively employed for image-to-image translation; however, their substantial computational and storage demands hinder deployment on mobile devices. Current network compression techniques primarily target visual recognition tasks, not generative applications. Our methodology introduces a knowledge distillation framework. A student generator, featuring fewer parameters, learns to mimic a larger teacher generator by inheriting its low-level and high-level information. To bolster the student generator's output quality, a dedicated student discriminator is incorporated. It quantifies discrepancies among real images, student-generated outputs, and teacher-generated images. An adversarial training process is subsequently established to jointly optimize both the student generator and its associated discriminator. Extensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations, conducted using standard benchmark datasets, validate that the method described yields compact generative models demonstrating robust performance.

author: Gaines
title: Automated Compression of BERT via Differentiable Neural Architecture Search for Task-Specific Adaption
abstract: Pre-trained language models, including large-scale BERT variants, exhibit considerable efficacy across diverse natural language processing domains. Nonetheless, their extensive parameter footprint poses significant obstacles for deployment in real-time settings demanding rapid inference on constrained computational resources. Current techniques for compressing BERT generate reduced models without considering task specifics; consequently, an identical compressed BERT serves all subsequent downstream applications. Recognizing the clear advantages and imperative for task-specific BERT compression, we introduce an innovative methodology. This approach employs differentiable Neural Architecture Search to autonomously create task-adapted small BERT models tailored for individual tasks. Our system integrates a task-specific knowledge distillation loss to guide the architectural search and an efficiency-centric loss, serving as a constraint. This dual objective ensures an advantageous balance between operational efficiency and model effectiveness during task-adaptive BERT compression. Evaluations of the proposed method were conducted across multiple NLP tasks. The outcomes indicate that the generated task-adaptive compressed models achieve inference speeds 12.7x to 29.3x higher than the full BERT model, and their parameter count is reduced by a factor of 11.5x to 17.0x, all while preserving comparable performance levels.

author: Harrell
title: Enabling Universal Participation in Federated Learning Across Diverse Hardware Capabilities
abstract: Federated learning (FL) offers a critical approach for constructing global models from distributed data while upholding privacy. Typically, current FL methodologies assume that any participating client can facilitate the training of the global model. However, real-world scenarios frequently involve heterogeneous client devices possessing varied computing power.
