Despite the immense success of large models such as BERT in artificial intelligence, their application becomes challenging within heterogeneous FL environments, particularly with weak clients. Simple solutions, like either excluding resource-constrained clients or employing a uniformly small model for all, introduce significant drawbacks, including under-representation of omitted clients or compromised accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. To address these issues, this work introduces a client-inclusive federated learning method. The core principle involves assigning models of different sizes to clients based on their specific computing capabilities, providing larger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. Additionally, an effective mechanism is proposed to facilitate knowledge sharing among these multiple local models, despite their varying sizes. This strategy ensures that all clients can contribute to the model learning process within FL, leading to a final model that is both extensive and robust. Furthermore, a momentum-based knowledge distillation technique is proposed to enhance the transfer of knowledge from large models operating on powerful clients to small models on weak clients. Comprehensive experimentation across numerous real-world benchmark datasets confirms the efficacy of this approach in developing accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

author: Evans
title: Developing Compact Evaluation Metrics for Machine Translation
abstract: Modern machine translation and multilingual text generation techniques have spurred the adoption of trained evaluation metrics. Examples like COMET or BLEURT frame assessment as a regression task, leveraging representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. However, research in similar domains indicates that optimal efficiency for these models typically requires substantial scale, which presents considerable cost and practical challenges in an evaluation setting. Our work examines the relationship between model capacity and multilingual capabilities. We employ RemBERT, a cutting-edge multilingual language model, utilizing datasets from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. A series of conducted experiments confirms that model dimensions indeed constrain performance during cross-lingual transfer. We then illustrate how knowledge distillation offers a solution to this constraint. Our approach involves generating synthetic data and transferring expertise from a single teacher model to several student models, each specialized in a set of related languages. This strategy results in performance gains of up to 10.5% compared to standard fine-tuning. Furthermore, our technique achieves 92.6% of RemBERT's effectiveness while requiring only one-third of its total parameters.

author: Fowler
title: Self-supervised Knowledge Distillation for Small Model Visual Representation
abstract: Empirical observations indicate that while contrastive self-supervised learning techniques are highly effective for training large models, their utility for smaller models is limited. This work addresses the specific challenge of applying self-supervised learning principles to architectures of reduced scale. To overcome this limitation, our methodology introduces a novel self-supervised distillation paradigm. This approach utilizes a larger network, serving as a Teacher, to transmit its representational knowledge to a smaller Student architecture, within a self-supervised framework. Rather than direct acquisition from unlabeled data, training involves instructing a student encoder to replicate the similarity score distribution generated by a Teacher across multiple instances. The proposed method substantially elevates the performance of small networks across various downstream tasks. When benchmarked against existing self-supervised approaches, top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet-1k dataset saw improvements from 42.2% to 67.6% for EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% for MobileNet-v3-Large.

author: Lynch
title: Learning Activity Recognition from Vision via Sensor-Based Knowledge Transfer
abstract: Improving accuracy in human activity recognition (HAR) has been recently achieved through multi-modal approaches. However, advanced methods employing multiple modalities are often incompatible with the limited computational resources inherent to wearable devices, such as smartwatches. To address this challenge, our work introduces an end-to-end knowledge distillation framework that transfers understanding from a vision domain to a sensor domain. This approach requires only time-series data, specifically accelerometer readings, from wearable devices during the inference phase, thereby significantly lowering computational demands on edge devices. Concurrently, the resulting distilled model is shown to achieve performance closely mirroring that of resource-intensive multi-modal methods. To preserve local temporal relationships and enable processing with visual deep learning architectures, time-series data is initially converted into two-dimensional image representations using the Gramian Angular Field (GAF) encoding technique. For the architecture, ResNet18 served as the teacher network, while a multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception was chosen as the student network. Furthermore, we propose a novel loss function, referred to as the Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss, designed to bridge the gap and mitigate variations between the visual and sensor modalities. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets confirm the efficacy and competitive performance of the proposed framework, underscoring its readiness for deployment on wearable sensors.

author: Hernandez
title: Accelerating Novel View Synthesis Through Neural Light Field Distillation from Neural Radiance Fields
abstract: Neural networks demonstrate considerable promise for depicting complex scenes, a potential strongly highlighted by the recent surge in Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) research. Nevertheless, NeRF models face a substantial limitation due to their excessive inference latency; rendering individual pixels demands hundreds of queries to the underlying network. Prior efforts to mitigate this primarily focus on decreasing the count of sampled points needed. Yet, the fundamental issue of repetitive sampling persists. Conversely, for novel view synthesis, Neural Light Field (NeLF) models offer a simpler representation compared to NeRF, where a single forward pass without ray-marching suffices to render any given pixel. This research introduces a deep residual multi-layer perceptron (MLP) architecture, comprising 88 layers, designed for robust light field learning. We establish that acquiring sufficient data is crucial for effectively training such an extensive NeLF network, a requirement met by transferring knowledge from an already-trained NeRF model through data distillation. Comprehensive evaluations across both synthetic and real-world environments demonstrate the advantages of this distillation approach when compared to alternative algorithms. Specifically, in synthetic scenarios, we observed a 26-35x reduction in FLOPs (per camera ray) and a 28-31x increase in runtime speed. Furthermore, the rendering quality was substantially superior, exhibiting a 1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement over NeRF, all without demanding any specialized parallelism.

author: Farmer
title: Optimizing 3D Object Detection Efficiency via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Advanced 3D object detectors frequently face significant computational demands, despite considerable progress within the domain. This work explores the application of knowledge distillation (KD) for constructing efficient 3D object detectors, specifically targeting popular architectures that utilize pillar and voxel representations. Initially, given the scarcity of well-defined teacher-student pairs, our investigation focuses on methods to derive student models presenting favorable trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency. This involves examining techniques such as model compression and reduced input resolution. Subsequently, we establish a benchmark to evaluate existing 2D KD methodologies for 3D object detection, built upon six meticulously crafted teacher-student pairings. A novel KD pipeline is also introduced, featuring two key innovations: an enhanced logit KD approach that restricts distillation to a limited number of critical positions identified by the teacher's classification response, and a teacher-guided initialization strategy for student models. This initialization aims to facilitate the transmission of the teacher model's feature extraction capabilities to students through weight inheritance. Extensive experiments conducted on the Waymo dataset confirm the efficacy of our approach. The top-performing configuration achieves 65.75% LEVEL 2 mAPH, surpassing its teacher model while consuming only 44% of the teacher's FLOPs. Our most efficient model processes 51 FPS on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, demonstrating a 2.2-fold speedup over PointPillar, alongside improved accuracy.

author: Ryan
title: Transferring Multi-Modal Network Expertise to Single-Modality Segmentation Systems
abstract: Recent investigations have extensively examined the combined utilization of various imaging modalities for medical image segmentation. The integration of data from diverse modalities has consistently demonstrated improved segmentation accuracy in several applications when contrasted with mono-modal segmentations. However, obtaining multiple modalities often proves impractical in clinical environments due to limited medical personnel and scanning equipment, along with the need to control expenses and scanning time. Most frequently, only a single modality is acquired. This publication details a framework designed for transferring knowledge from a pre-trained multi-modal network (functioning as the teacher) to a mono-modal network (acting as the student). The presented technique is an adaptation of the generalized distillation paradigm, where the student network undergoes training using a single modality, representing a portion of the teacher's total 'n' input modalities. We validate the framework's performance on brain tumor segmentation, employing the BraTS 2018 dataset. Employing distinct network architectures, our results confirm that the student network acquires knowledge effectively from the teacher, invariably surpassing the performance of the foundational mono-modal network regarding segmentation accuracy.

author: Osborne
title: Extracting Learnings from Advanced Neural Networks for Healthcare Applications
abstract: The rapid expansion of Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has generated significant opportunities and a critical demand for identifying useful data-driven disease representations and patterns within the field of Computational Phenotyping. While Deep Learning models demonstrate excellent capabilities for robust prediction in computational phenotyping scenarios, their lack of model interpretability poses a substantial challenge, particularly for clinicians who require transparent insights for decision-making processes. This article presents an innovative knowledge-distillation methodology, herein referred to as "the proposed method," designed to acquire interpretable phenotype features that facilitate robust predictions by emulating the performance of deep learning models. The architecture of this framework employs Gradient Boosting Trees for extracting interpretable features derived from deep learning models, including Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Comprehensive evaluations conducted on a real-world clinical time-series dataset indicate that the proposed method achieves performance levels comparable to or exceeding those of the deep learning models, concurrently supplying interpretable phenotypes critical for clinical decision making.

author: Moreno
title: Developing Visually-Informed Rapid Quadrotor Control in Densely Cluttered Settings
abstract: For autonomous quadrotor navigation in complex, obstructed settings, achieving minimal transit times, contemporary neural control policies surpass conventional model-based planning techniques. Nevertheless, these approaches lack awareness of perception capabilities, a vital aspect for systems relying on camera input, given the restricted field of view inherent to cameras and the underactuated characteristics of quadrotors. To address this deficit, we introduce a learning-driven framework that facilitates high-agility quadrotor flight within visually challenging environments, while maintaining awareness of visual input limitations. This approach integrates reinforcement learning (RL) and imitation learning, utilizing a specialized setup where complete state information is available during training. Initially, an RL-based teacher policy is developed, which benefits from full-state information and is specifically designed for perception awareness, enabling it to navigate through dense clutter with minimal time expenditure. Subsequently, this teacher's expertise is transferred via imitation learning to a student policy; this student operates solely on visual data acquired from a camera, making it vision-based. The methodology effectively integrates perception and control, yielding substantial performance benefits, notably a tenfold increase in computational velocity and an enhanced success rate. Validation of the closed-loop control efficacy was conducted through hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

author: Smith
title: Approach to Engineer Small, Fast, and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domain-Specific Use
abstract: While large pre-trained models have achieved notable success across many general natural language processing tasks, their application in specialized fields introduces challenges. These include issues stemming from domain shift, difficulties during fine-tuning, and constraints on latency and capacity for online serving. This paper introduces a versatile methodology for constructing small, rapid, and highly effective pre-trained models tailored for specific domains. Our strategy involves adapting existing general pre-trained models and then applying task-agnostic knowledge distillation within the target domain contexts. More specifically, the adaptation stage incorporates domain-specific vocabulary expansion, where the size of the incremental vocabulary is automatically determined by corpus-level occurrence probability. Subsequently, we systematically investigate various techniques to compress the extensive pre-trained models for their domain-specific deployments. Our empirical evaluations were conducted in the biomedical and computer science domains. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms the BERT BASE model on domain-specific tasks, while simultaneously being 3.3 times smaller and 5.1 times faster than BERT BASE. The source code and pre-trained models are accessible at https://aka.ms/adalm.

author: Nguyen
title: Improving Parameter-Efficient Highway Networks with Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deep learning has delivered substantial advances in speech recognition over recent years. Nevertheless, neural network models typically require significantly more parameters than conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, thus hindering their deployment on embedded devices. Our prior research explored a compact class of depth-gated feedforward neural networks, termed highway deep neural networks (HDNNs), for acoustic modeling. This investigation demonstrated that HDNN-based acoustic models could achieve recognition performance comparable to plain deep neural networks (DNNs) while utilizing considerably fewer model parameters. This current work extends these efforts by applying the knowledge distillation technique, also known as teacher-student training. Specifically, we trained the compact HDNN model under the guidance of a highly accurate, yet computationally demanding, model. Furthermore, we examined sequence training and adaptation within this teacher-student framework. Experiments were conducted using the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. Through this methodology, we substantially boosted the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model, which has fewer than 0.8 million parameters. This effectively narrowed the performance difference between this compact model and a plain DNN containing 30 million parameters.
